title: Chapter 10.  Article 35A — Permanent Residents, Property Rights & Its Controversy

blocks.content: Article 35A is frequently tested alongside Article 370 but is legally and historically distinct — candidates should be able to explain exactly what 35A did, how it was created, and why it became one of the most legally contested provisions of the Indian Constitution before both were removed together in 2019.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 35A was incorporated into the Indian Constitution via a Presidential Order in 1954 under Article 370.
It empowered the Jammu & Kashmir State Legislature to define 'permanent residents' of the state.
Permanent residents enjoyed exclusive rights regarding state employment, acquisition of immovable property, and government scholarships.
Non-permanent residents were barred from acquiring land or settling permanently in the state.
Article 35A was rendered inoperative on August 5, 2019, along with the abrogation of Article 370.

blocks.content: Article 35A was inserted into the Constitution of India via the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954 — a Presidential Order issued under the authority of Article 370 — rather than through the standard Parliamentary constitutional-amendment procedure under Article 368, a procedural fact that became central to later legal challenges against its validity.
Article 35A — Permanent Residents, Property Rights & Its Controversy

The Article empowered the J&K state legislature to define who qualified as a 'Permanent Resident' of the state, and to confer upon such Permanent Residents special rights and privileges regarding: (a) employment under the state government, (b) acquisition of immovable property within the state, (c) settlement in the state, and (d) scholarships and other forms of state aid — while, correspondingly, permitting the legislature to restrict these rights for non-Permanent Residents (including other Indian citizens from outside the state).

In practical effect, Article 35A meant that Indian citizens from other states could not purchase land or immovable property in J&K, could not obtain permanent state-government jobs, and — most controversially in later social/legal debate — that women from J&K who married men from outside the state risked losing their own Permanent Resident status and, by extension, their children's inheritance/property rights within the state (a provision that was itself later softened by a 2002 J&K High Court ruling clarifying that women did not lose their Permanent Resident status upon marrying outside the state, though the status of their children remained contested).

cells: Constitution (Application to J&K) Order, 1954 (a Presidential Order under Article 370, not a formal Article 368 amendment)
Empowered the J&K legislature to define 'Permanent Residents' and grant them exclusive rights over state employment, property acquisition, settlement, and scholarships/state aid
Non-Permanent Residents (including other Indian citizens) could not purchase immovable property or hold permanent state-government jobs in J&K

Women marrying outside the state risked losing Permanent Resident status; a 2002 J&K High Court ruling held that women retained their status even after marrying a non-Permanent Resident, though ambiguity around children's status persisted

rows: Allowed to purchase and own property

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Article 35A was NOT itself a formally numbered constitutional amendment passed by Parliament — it was inserted via a Presidential Order under Article 370's authority. This procedural distinction (Presidential Order vs. Article 368 amendment) was the central legal argument used by later petitioners challenging its constitutional validity.

items: From around 2014 onward, several petitions were filed before the Supreme Court of India challenging Article 35A's constitutional validity, primarily on the grounds that it had been introduced through an executive Presidential Order rather than the formal Parliamentary amendment process required for altering fundamental rights, and that it discriminated against non-residents and, in its practical operation, against women.

Supporters of Article 35A — including a broad cross-section of J&K's mainstream political parties across the ideological spectrum — argued that the provision was essential to protect the state's unique demographic character, land, and local employment opportunities for its own residents, particularly given the region's small population and land area relative to the rest of India, and that any judicial or legislative move to dilute it risked altering the region's demographic composition.

These legal challenges to Article 35A remained pending before the Supreme Court and were never definitively resolved by judicial verdict; the issue instead became moot in practical terms following the government's 2019 abrogation of Article 370 (Chapter 13), which rendered Article 35A automatically inoperative as well, since it had been dependent on Article 370's continued existence.
Article 35A was added via Presidential Order (1954), not through a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368.
It was inextricably linked to Article 370 and was revoked on August 5, 2019.
Questions frequently test the distinction between general constitutional provisions and the exclusive property rights restricted by Article 35A.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Article 35A's legal challenges were NEVER decided by the Supreme Court on their merits — the provision was rendered moot by the 2019 abrogation of Article 370 itself, since 35A had been introduced under 370's authority. This is a frequently mis-stated point; candidates should say the issue became 'moot', not that the Court 'struck down' 35A.

items: Article 35A inserted via the Constitution (Application to J&K) Order, 1954 — a Presidential Order under Article 370, not a formal Article 368 amendment.
Granted J&K's legislature power to define 'Permanent Residents' and reserve state jobs, property rights, settlement, and scholarships for them.
Non-residents (including other Indian citizens) could not buy property or hold permanent state jobs in J&K under this provision.
2002 J&K High Court ruling: women retain Permanent Resident status after marrying outside the state.
Legal challenges to Article 35A (from ~2014) were never decided on merits by the Supreme Court — the provision became moot after the 2019 abrogation of Article 370.
